issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: For a witnessed-other trauma, strong flashback-like re-experiencing can occur, but this specific item implies reliving as if the traumatic experience were happening to the patient directly. With the rest of the profile emphasizing fragmented narrative memory and indirect threat cues, this item is somewhat mismatched to the witnessed-trauma context and is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to reconcile with a witnessed-other trauma unless there was clear perceived responsibility or preventability. No other items suggest responsibility, guilt about failing to intervene, or action-related causation, so this appraisal is insufficiently supported by the rest of the profile.

Clinical Vignette: Mei Chen

Mei Chen was sixty-one years old when she came to the clinic, though her face bore the particular exhaustion of someone who had spent months-perhaps years-holding her breath. She was a sculptor, known in her Seattle community for intricate wooden pieces that seemed to breathe with their own life, though she had barely touched her tools in the past eighteen months. Her hands, still capable and strong, had grown still.

The trauma that had reshaped her life occurred on a March evening two years ago at a gallery opening. Mei had been standing near the entrance, speaking with a colleague about an upcoming commission, when the man beside her-a gallery patron she did not know-had suffered a sudden, catastrophic stroke. She watched him collapse, watched his face contort as his body seized, watched the paramedics work on him across the marble floor while guests stood frozen around her. The man died in the ambulance. Mei had not known him. She had simply been there.

In the weeks that followed, she had tried to return to normal. Her husband, David, had been supportive, patient. But something had fractured inside her that could not be easily repaired. The first sign was the perfume. A woman at the grocery store had worn the same cologne the gallery patron had been wearing that evening-a sharp, woody scent that Mei had noticed only in retrospect, only after she understood that she would carry every detail of his dying with her forever. When she encountered that smell again, her heart had seized in her chest. The memory had flooded back with such force and vividness that she could not distinguish it from the present moment; she was there again, watching the man's eyes roll back, and the grocery store dissolved into that terrible gallery space. The memory felt more real, more immediate, than the fluorescent lights and shopping carts around her. After that, she had begun to avoid places where she might encounter unexpected scents, and the avoidance had only deepened her conviction that the world was fundamentally unpredictable and dangerous-that safety was an illusion, and that she could not trust her own body to protect her from being ambushed by horror.

Footsteps behind her now sent her into a state of high alert. On walks with David, she would turn around repeatedly, her shoulders tense, her breath shallow. Unpredictable situations-a knock on the door, a change in plans, even a phone call from an unknown number-triggered a startle response so violent that David had learned to announce himself before entering rooms. At night, the vigilance intensified. Mei lay awake, listening, certain that danger was present in the darkness even though she could not name what she feared. Her body would jolt at sounds-the house settling, a car passing-and she would lie rigid, her heart pounding, unable to return to sleep. The threat felt constant, imminent, as though the collapse she had witnessed was a prophecy of collapse everywhere, in everyone.

When she tried to explain what had happened to David or to herself, the narrative fractured. She could describe the gallery, the smell of the cologne, the moment of the collapse, but the pieces would not cohere into a story. She would lose the thread mid-sentence, unable to articulate why the memory felt so invasive, so inescapable. This fragmentation reinforced her growing conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with her-that she was broken in some essential way, that a normal person would have moved past this by now, that her inability to construct a coherent narrative was evidence of her own defectiveness. These thoughts, once lodged, began to poison everything. If she was defective, then how could she trust her own judgment? How could she trust anyone else's? The world, which had always felt reasonably safe, now seemed populated by hidden threats and unreliable people. Her husband's reassurances, meant to comfort her, instead triggered a deeper mistrust; she found herself wondering if he was simply being kind, if he secretly thought she was falling apart, if anyone could really be trusted to tell the truth.

The vivid, intrusive memories had become the engine of her suffering. When a memory surfaced-triggered by a sound, a scent, an unexpected moment-it would generate a cascade of physical reactivity: her chest would tighten, her hands would tremble, sweat would bead on her forehead. These physical reactions would themselves become triggers, reminding her of her vulnerability, which would then intensify her threat perception and pull her further into the conviction that the world was dangerous and that she could not be trusted to navigate it safely. She had stopped accepting gallery invitations. She had stopped going to restaurants. She had begun to avoid even the studio where her sculptures waited, because the smell of the wood and the solvent she used had somehow become entangled with the gallery smell, with the memory, with the fear.

What finally brought Mei to seek help was David's quiet observation that she was disappearing. Not dramatically, but incrementally-fewer phone calls to friends, fewer reasons to leave the house, fewer moments when she seemed present even when she was in the room. She was sixty-one years old and terrified that the rest of her life would be lived in this contracted space, held hostage by a memory that would not release her and a conviction that she was fundamentally broken. She wanted to sculpt again. She wanted to walk without scanning for threats. She wanted, most of all, to trust that her mind would not betray her with intrusions she could not control.
